strengths: Addresses practical and relevant problem of defending MAS against unknown attacks without labeled data
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 topologies, 3 attack types, and multiple LLM backbones with consistent results
Well-motivated design with clear identification of gaps in existing unsupervised GAD methods for MAS
Intuitive hierarchical encoder design (self/neighbor/global levels) validated through ablation study
Clear presentation with effective visual explanations of the methodology
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (hierarchical GNNs, contrastive learning, noise-based corruption) without significant methodological innovation

Core assumption unvalidated: synthetic Gaussian noise in embedding space may not capture semantic structure of real attacks (prompt injection, memory poisoning); no evidence provided that corruption reflects actual attack patterns
Claims about defending 'unknown attacks' are overstated; evaluation only tests three known attack types without any held-out attack types to validate true generalization to unseen attacks
Substantial performance gap with supervised baseline: BlindGuard achieves 75-85% AUC in many scenarios while G-Safeguard achieves 90-100%, which is significant for security-critical applications

Incomplete analysis: significant performance variation across topologies (e.g., 69.33% vs 59.55% vs 70.22% on GSM8K) lacks explanation; no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters α and K; missing comparisons with simpler baselines
Threat model and adversarial robustness not addressed: no analysis of gradual attacks, adaptive attackers aware of defense mechanism, or evasion strategies

Reproducibility concerns: key design choices unexplained (why freeze SentenceBERT?), MLP architecture unspecified, hyperparameter sensitivity not analyzed, unclear how much clean training data is needed
Limited scalability validation: tested only to 50 agents without computational cost analysis; claim of 'topology-agnostic design' not rigorously validated

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: unsupervised defense for MAS deployments without labeled malicious agent data
Clearly identifies and articulates specific gaps in existing GAD methods (multi-level contextual awareness and semantic anomaly assumptions)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 attack types, 4 topologies, 3 LLM backbones, and 5 datasets with scalability testing
Strong empirical results showing competitive performance against unsupervised baselines and approaching supervised baseline across diverse settings
Clear technical presentation with detailed algorithms, ablation studies, and commitment to reproducibility via code release
Sensible hierarchical design that integrates agent-level, neighborhood, and system-level information
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: hierarchical encoding is straightforward concatenation + MLP; contrastive learning and noise injection are well-established techniques applied with minimal innovation

Core assumption never validated: claims that real semantic attacks can be simulated via random magnitude-scaled noise in embedding space lacks theoretical justification or empirical evidence (no representation space analysis, visualization of synthetic vs. real attacks)
Attack heterogeneity ignored: prompt injection, memory poisoning, and tool exploitation likely produce distinct semantic perturbations, yet corruption function applies uniform random noise

Experimental rigor concerns: no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds; unfair comparison with supervised G-Safeguard; weak baselines (generic GAD methods not designed for MAS)
Design choices poorly justified: why negative average similarity for inference? Why concatenation for feature fusion? Sensitivity to critical hyperparameter α (corruption intensity) never explored

Generalization claims lack support: training data quality/diversity never discussed; no evaluation against adaptive attacks; no analysis of how method degrades with limited or non-representative normal training data
Insufficient analysis of why it works: missing error analysis showing which attack types/topologies fail; representation space clustering not visualized; no comparison of corruption strategies
Frozen SentenceBERT encoder prevents adaptation to MAS-specific language patterns; remediation strategy borrowed directly from G-Safeguard without innovation
Gap to supervised baseline remains substantial (AUC ~80% vs. 95-100% for G-Safeguard); writing overclaims 'universal' performance and 'competitive' results relative to this gap
Missing practical guidance: no justification for hyperparameter choices; unclear how to select K (malicious agents budget) and corruption subset fraction in deployment

Clearly articulated research gaps and well-justified hierarchical encoder design capturing multi-level MAS interaction patterns
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions (3 attack types, 4 topologies, 3 LLM backbones, scalability to 50 agents)
Strong empirical results consistently competitive with supervised upper bound G-Safeguard and outperforming unsupervised baselines
Demonstrated generalizability with a single trained model working across different attack types and LLM backbones
Good reproducibility with code availability and detailed implementation specifications
Clear presentation with effective motivation figures and well-structured methodology section
weaknesses: Core assumption linking synthetic noise-based corruptions to real semantic attacks (deceptive intent, poisoning) lacks empirical validation; no evidence that directional noise injection matches actual attack perturbation patterns
Absence of adversarial evaluation against adaptive attacks; all evaluated attacks are straightforward implementations without consideration of adaptive adversaries
Critical hyperparameters (corruption intensity α, K=3 budget, R=3 rounds) appear arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis or justification
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or clarity on single-run vs. multi-seed averaging
Incomplete hyperparameter analysis: no investigation of how corruption intensity should vary across attack types or MAS configurations
Vague training data requirements claim ('small amount') without sensitivity analysis or minimum data thresholds; scalability with data constraints unclear
Limited novelty in individual components (hierarchical GNN encoding, contrastive learning, synthetic sample generation are established techniques)
Failure mode analysis absent: no discussion of when/why BlindGuard underperforms or against what attack characteristics it is vulnerable
Lack of theoretical justification for why synthetic contrastive learning should transfer to real attacks; synthetic-to-real gap is empirical but unexplained
Baselines are general GAD methods not designed for MAS; only MAS-specific baseline (G-Safeguard) is supervised making comparisons potentially unfair

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: Identifies genuine gap in existing MAS defenses that require labeled malicious data, with clear motivation for unsupervised approach

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple attack types, topologies, LLM backbones, and robustness tests (collusion, adaptive attacks, scalability to 50 agents, attack-free scenarios)
Thoughtful system design: Hierarchical encoder effectively combines agent-level, neighborhood, and global context; corruption-guided contrastive learning is well-suited to unsupervised setting
Strong empirical results: Consistently outperforms unsupervised baselines and achieves competitive AUC with supervised methods; demonstrates superior cross-attack generalization
Honest limitations disclosure: Clearly documents failure modes (manifold-preserving attacks, benign heterogeneity) with concrete analysis in Appendix I, showing research integrity
weaknesses: Unvalidated core assumption: Directional Gaussian noise in embedding space as proxy for real attacks is intuitive but not rigorously validated; gap between synthetic corruption and diverse real-world attacks (PI, memory poisoning, tool exploitation) not theoretically justified

Limited evaluation against sophisticated adversaries: Experiments mostly against straightforward attacks; only one simple adaptive attack tested; no evaluation against adversaries aware of defense trying to minimize semantic deviation

Detection budget K must be known: All experiments assume exactly K=3 malicious agents (actual test set size); threshold-based variants (Table 6) still require calibration; practical limitation not adequately discussed
Moderate technical novelty: Hierarchical encoding is straightforward feature concatenation; contrastive learning is established; main contribution is combination rather than methodological innovation

Insufficient theoretical grounding: No analysis of what attack properties method can/cannot detect; no formal guarantees or characterization of when synthetic corruption correlates with real attacks; Appendix H acknowledges limitation without resolution

Overstated generalization claims: 'Attack-agnostic' terminology misleading as method learns from specific task behaviors; cross-attack generalization shown only on CSQA; unclear generalization to tasks with different reasoning patterns
Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; unclear if single runs or multiple seeds; cannot assess result stability
Incomplete scalability analysis: O(N²d) complexity mentioned but proposed mitigations (block-wise computation, top-k pruning) not evaluated; unclear scaling to hundreds of agents

strengths: Well-motivated shift from supervised to unsupervised MAS defense with practical justification
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple attack types, topologies, and LLMs with extensive ablations
Hierarchical encoder design (ego/neighbor/global features) is intuitive and empirically validated through ablation study (Figure 5)
Interesting result demonstrating unsupervised models generalize to unseen attack types better than supervised baselines (Table 2)
Honest acknowledgment of limitations and failure modes in Section I, including susceptibility to on-topic stealthy attacks
weaknesses: Core technical assumption is questionable: random directional noise in embedding space poorly captures structured semantic effects of real attacks; failure analysis (Section I) admits stealthy on-topic attacks bypass the detector, undermining the approach

Evaluation limited to simulated environments with fixed K=3 malicious agents and artificially constructed attacks; no statistical significance testing, error bars, or multi-seed variance analysis; unclear real-world applicability
Limited technical novelty: hierarchical GNN encoding + supervised contrastive learning are standard components; main contribution is their combination for MAS, which is incremental

Unfair baseline comparisons: DOMINANT, PREM, TAM were not designed for MAS; stronger graph anomaly detection methods not adapted or compared; performance gaps often small and lack statistical validation

Disconnect between motivation and solution: claimed 'semantic anomalies' are addressed via random embedding corruption (Gap 2), a mismatch acknowledged but not resolved; Section I confirms this fundamental weakness
Scalability concerns: O(N²d) anomaly scoring complexity; mentioned optimizations (block-wise, top-k) not implemented or evaluated; testing limited to 50 agents

Hyperparameter tuning underexplored: corruption intensity α requires manual selection (range 0.3–0.8); no analysis of sensitivity to other training hyperparameters or practical guidance for practitioners

Generalization claims overstated: cross-attack evaluation limited to single direction (PI→MA on CSQA); failure analysis directly contradicts robust generalization; method struggles precisely with attacks sophisticated adversaries would deploy
Reproducibility gaps: code unavailable for review; exact dataset construction not fully specified; prompt structures not explicitly shown; no discussion of random seeds or variance

Presentation issues: Figure 2 overcrowded and poorly explained; key details relegated to appendix; some claims overstate evidence (e.g., 'competitive performance' masks large AUC gaps like 75.11 vs. 99.11)

strengths: Practical problem formulation: Addresses real limitation of supervised defenses by proposing unsupervised paradigm that doesn't require labeled malicious agents, making it applicable to real-world MAS deployments

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation: 3 attack types × 4 topologies × 3 LLM backbones, with extensive ablations (collusion attacks, adaptive attacks, encoder analysis, attack-free evaluation, scalability to 50 agents)

Strong empirical results: Significantly outperforms unsupervised baselines (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM), achieves competitive AUC>80% with supervised baseline G-Safeguard, and demonstrates superior generalization to unseen attack types

Clear technical design with well-motivated gaps: Hierarchical encoder (addressing multi-level awareness) and corruption-guided detector (addressing semantic vs. structural assumptions) are intuitive and properly justified
Responsible research practices: Acknowledges limitations transparently, provides failure case analysis, discusses false positives/negatives, and promises code release for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Primarily combines existing techniques (hierarchical GNNs, supervised contrastive learning, directional noise injection) for MAS domain rather than developing fundamentally new methods

Unvalidated core assumption: The directional noise corruption strategy (Eq. 5) is ad-hoc and lacks rigorous validation that synthetic corruptions actually approximate real malicious behaviors across diverse attack types; reliance on assumption that semantic attacks manifest as angular deviations may not hold generally

Limited attack scope and identified failure modes: Only 3 semantic-level attacks tested; Appendix I candidly identifies vulnerabilities to stealthy on-topic attacks that remain semantically aligned (false negatives) and benign agents with atypical reasoning styles (false positives)

Evaluation restricted to simulation: All experiments on simulated MAS environments with no real-world validation; real systems may exhibit different failure modes, attack vectors, or communication patterns, limiting practical impact claims

Insufficient baseline comparisons: Compared methods are generic GAD methods not designed for MAS; only one MAS-specific baseline (G-Safeguard, supervised); missing comparisons with other unsupervised MAS defenses or simpler alternatives
Theoretical understanding gaps: No formal analysis of when/why method works or fails, no detection guarantees, decision boundary characterization is primarily empirical

Artificial experimental constraints: Fixed budget K=3 assumes knowledge of exact number of malicious agents; main results rely on this prior even though threshold-based variant is tested; real scenarios have unknown K

Incomplete practical analysis: Limited exploration of utility-security tradeoff beyond accuracy; no analysis of how prompt structures or agent roles affect detection; missing guidance on choosing corruption ratio in practice
